131843	definition of a sigmet	D283991	Accidents during cruise are almost unheard of in turbine airplanes where the risk is concentrated in the departure and arrival phases of flight.
General aviation pilots also come to grief most frequently in the airport vicinity
column2: but an alarming number of accidents happen during cruise
column3: which should be a benign part of any trip.

column1: Most serious accidents in cruise involve bad weather.
The less serious events usually are caused by a loss of power
column2: typically because there is no fuel on board
column3: or the fuel that is there isn't reaching the engine.

column1: And there are several accidents every year that remain total mysteries.
In these cases the pilot is usually flying VFR
column2: not in contact with controllers
column3: and the wreckage is found sometime later after a search is launched when the airplane is reported missing.

column1: That type of crash leaves very few clues to determine a probable cause.
Twenty to 30 years ago the so-called continued VFR accident was among the most common type of serious crash.

The non-instrument rated pilot would plunge ahead into deteriorating weather conditions and be forced to fly lower and lower to stay out of the clouds until he flew into something he could no longer see.
The FAA and general aviation industry believed that expanding the number of instrument rated pilots would solve the continued VFR accident problem.
Now well over half of all pilots are IFR rated.
The total experience required to earn the rating was reduced and pilots are encouraged to add the IFR rating as soon as possible after earning the private license.
Years ago it was the reverse when most would advance to a commercial certificate before tackling instrument training.

column2: the plan worked
column3: but not in a way anyone intended.

column1: Now accidents that occur when IFR pilots are flying in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) outnumber the classic continued VFR accident.
And the results of a loss of control in the clouds are almost always fatal while the scud-running VFR pilot does have a chance to put it down somewhere before losing all contact with the ground.
Avoiding a continued VFR accident is the easiest thing in the world because you have a continuous real-time weather report right in front of you.
No matter what the forecast says
column2: no matter what weather stations are reporting
column3: the only weather report that matters to a VFR pilot is what you see out the windshield.

column1: When pilots used to routinely fly long trips VFR the experienced among them developed rules for when to call it quits.

column2: over flat lands if you never cruise below 1
column3: 000 feet your chances of survival are good.

column1: Obstacles such as antennas are still a problem
column2: but they are well charted and if you land before visibility drops you will be able to see and avoid obstacles.

column1: Over lumpy terrain the smart pilot won't continue if he can't see at least the next two
column2: or better three

column1: If visibility drops to the point that you can only see the next ridge to cross
column2: you have no way of knowing if the hill behind that is hidden in the clouds.

column1: But when you can see multiple ridges you know you can continue
column2: and better still
column3: know that there is enough visibility to turn around when you can see the ridges ahead.

column1: Of course scud running in the high mountains of the west is just plain suicide.
The terrain is often so steep
column2: and the valleys so deep
column3: that there is no escape and no way to see beyond the peaks.

column1: But flying IFR in IMC is different.
You shouldn't need to see the ground or a horizon to control the airplane
column2: but there are clouds that can make it very demanding to maintain control of a general aviation airplane.

column1: Thunderstorms and ice are the two big worries for every IFR pilot
column2: but there are turbulent clouds that can toss piston singles and twins around without being convective.

column1: I am lucky enough to get to fly both jets and piston airplanes
column2: and in a bumpy cloud it is much easier to control a jet with its higher wing loading.

column1: Turbulence that makes the piston airplane wallow and roll is usually converted into short
column2: sharp jolts by the speed and high wing loading of the jet.

column1: The rapidly rising air of a mountain wave or unstable cloud can push the light airplane up
column2: and then down
column3: for long periods while the pilot has to fly unnatural pitch attitudes to maintain assigned altitude.

column1: But those phenomenon are barely noticeable in a jet.
Nobody knows for sure how big a part turbulence plays in the loss of control by IFR pilots
column2: but I suspect it is large.

column1: Flying IFR in smooth stratus clouds is easy because the airplane deviates little from straight and level.

But in big bumps flying IFR in a light airplane you must perform an almost continuous upset recovery maneuver because the airplane can easily be displaced by many degrees of pitch and roll before you can move the controls to correct back.
The best way to maintain control in IMC in cruise is to have an autopilot and use it.
No matter how bumpy it gets the autopilot is making corrections instantly.
It takes time for the airplane to respond to the control inputs
column2: but the autopilot doesn't become disoriented.

column1: For some reason many general aviation pilots don't rely on their autopilots enough and even turn them off when they are most useful
column2: such as in a bumpy cloud or on a low approach.

column1: Turning the autopilot off in bad weather conditions would be like kicking the copilot out of a jet when things got bad.
You want all of the help you can get.
The old advice on autopilot use in turbulence was to turn off the altitude hold function and let the airplane move up and down.
That was probably a good technique except many modern autopilots hold a set pitch attitude no matter whether altitude hold mode is engaged or not.

column2: it doesn't matter whether the autopilot is holding a target pitch attitude
column4: the result is the same in turbulence
column5: so you may as well leave it in altitude hold mode.

column1: The autopilot will use some rather large pitch changes to hold altitude or attitude so you need to monitor airspeed and adjust power to keep the speed under control.
It's vital to fully understand how your autopilot functions because there are wide differences from one system to another.

column2: the autopilot systems in most general aviation airplanes are single string
column3: meaning that there are several points where failure disables the whole system.

column2: there is only one computer

column1: There are only single servos to move the control surfaces in each axis.

column2: the human remains the backup for them and needs to be ready to take over.

column1: The most important part of maintaining control in turbulent clouds is to work hard at keeping the wings level.
It is virtually impossible to lose control when the wings are level because the stability of the airplane keeps trying to bring the pitch attitude back to match the trimmed airspeed.

column2: try pushing or pulling on the controls with the wings level in VFR conditions.

column1: It will take a great deal of effort on the controls to make big changes in the airspeed in either direction.
Now try the same thing in a steep bank and you will find that pulling hard without feeding in opposite aileron only steepens the bank and increases airspeed.
In a steep bank any release of back pressure on the wheel will allow the nose to drop and increase airspeed.

Q: I have an overnight layover in Paris arriving at 8pm and leaving at 9:30am the next day.

A-1: The Eiffel Tower is about 26 miles (42 kms) from the CDG airport There is a metro (rer) from the airport but you will have to make some connections.

Taxis are on meters and should run round trip about 100 --140 euros

Role of the calcium ions in muscle cx • Ca++ binds to the Troponin molecules in the actin filaments • The troponin pushes tropomyosin off of actin's myosin binding sites • This frees the actin molecules to bind to the myosin heads

The contraction: steps involved • The head of a myosin molecule is activated by ATP • The myosin head bends • The head binds to the now uncovered binding site on the actin molecule • The myosin head changes shape and pulls the actin filament • This is called the POWER STROKE • The actin filament slides towards the center of the sarcomere
During a muscle contraction the actin filaments slide together and the myosin heads bend and pull.
What happens to the rest of the myosin filament?
The myosin filaments do not move.
Only the heads bend and pull on the actin.

Breaking the myosin bond • A new ATP molecule binds to the myosin head • The myosin head breaks its bond with actin • Myosin must receive a new ATP in order to break its bond with actin • The myosin head then Grabs another actin molecule further along on the actin filament • Again the myosin changes shape and pulls the actin filament closer to the center of the sarcomere • The process repeats until all of the Ca++ has been reabsorbed into the sarcoplasmic reticulumwhen calcium is no longer present... the troponin slides back to recover the myosin binding site on the actin molecule This makes it impossible for the myosin heads to bind to any other actin

Purpose of Salvation Army bands today  [ edit]The primary purpose of all Salvation Army bands is to serve as an instrument to proclaim the Christian gospel.
All other activities and functions of the band are only considered proper when this ultimate goal is observed.

column1: Music is also a means to attract and hold members to the movement.
Many individuals were originally introduced to The Salvation Army through the music programs.
Others would have strayed from the cause if not for their interest in brass bands.
Service provided by musicians often far exceeds just playing an instrument - most band members also serve in other roles in the corps.
The brass band is also an excellent means of drawing attention for fund-raising and publicity.
Participation in public and civic events raises awareness of The Salvation Army and its mission in many communities.
The brass band also provides a source of fellowship for the players.
